- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.4) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 2–5% relative to prior period.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior day), model often overshoots in next 3–5 days; apply downward correction of 3–8% to avoid overreaction.
- If sentiment is high (≥0.8) and price is trending up, model frequently overcorrects; cap forecast at 1–2% above recent high or adjust downward if sentiment drops.
- When sentiment is volatile or mixed (0.2–0.6), model exhibits mean-reversion bias; smooth forecast by averaging 3–5 prior days’ values or apply 1–3% dampening.
- For 30-day horizon, model often underestimates downward trends; if sentiment is negative or price is falling, add 1–3% buffer to forecast to account for lag.
- If sentiment is high but price is flat or declining, model tends to overpredict; reduce forecast by 1–4% to align with sentiment divergence.
- When sentiment is low and price is rising, model often fails to recognize momentum; increase forecast by 1–3% to reflect sentiment lag.
